blocks.text: A child's top spinning on its tip leans over yet does not fall: it swings slowly round in a circle instead. A turbine rotor on a turning vehicle shoves its bearings sideways even though nothing seems to push on it. Both are the same fact: changing the direction of a spinning body's angular momentum needs a torque, and the body pushes back with an equal and opposite one.

blocks.markdown: A rotor of moment of inertia $I$ (kg m$^2$) about its spin axis, spinning at $\omega$ (rad/s), has angular momentum $\mathbf H=I\boldsymbol\omega$ pointing along the axis by the right-hand rule. If the axis is turned at angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega_p$ (the **precession**), the tip of $\mathbf H$ moves with velocity $\boldsymbol\omega_p\times\mathbf H$. By Newton's second law for rotation, the torque on the rotor must equal this rate of change of $\mathbf H$.

blocks.latex: \mathbf M_{\text{on rotor}}=\boldsymbol\omega_p\times\mathbf H,\qquad C=I\omega\,\omega_p\ \ (\text{for perpendicular axes})
blocks.caption: The rotor exerts the reaction couple $-\boldsymbol\omega_p\times\mathbf H$ on its bearings and frame.

blocks.title: Gyroscopic couple
blocks.text: The **gyroscopic couple** is the torque $C=I\omega\omega_p$ (N m) needed to precess a spinning rotor, applied by the bearings. The **gyroscopic reaction** on the bearings is equal and opposite. If the spin and precession axes are parallel, $\boldsymbol\omega_p\times\mathbf H=0$ and there is no couple; the effect is largest when the axes are at $90^\circ$.

blocks.title: Size of the couple
blocks.prompt: A disc rotor ($I=0.12$ kg m$^2$) turns at 3000 rev/min and its axis is turned perpendicular to itself at 0.8 rad/s. Find the gyroscopic couple.
blocks.answer: $C=30.2$ N m, even though the rotor is small. The couple is proportional to the product of spin and precession rates.

blocks.markdown: **Direction.** Use vectors, not intuition. (1) Draw $\mathbf H$ along the axis by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers in the spin direction, thumb points along $\mathbf H$. (2) Draw $\boldsymbol\omega_p$ for the turning of the axis, again by the right-hand rule. (3) The torque on the rotor is $\boldsymbol\omega_p\times\mathbf H$. (4) The reaction on the bearings and frame is the opposite vector. The couple axis is perpendicular to both the spin axis and the precession axis.

blocks.title: Ship pitching: which way does the bow yaw?
blocks.prompt: A turbine rotor has its angular momentum $\mathbf H$ pointing toward the bow. Take $x$ forward, $y$ to port, $z$ up. The bow rises (pitches up). Find the direction of the reaction couple on the ship.

steps.text: Bow up is rotation about the starboard axis, so the precession vector is $-\omega_p\hat j$ (rotation about $+\hat j$ lowers the bow).
Reaction on the ship is opposite, i.e. $-\hat k$, a clockwise yaw viewed from above.

blocks.answer: The reaction tends to yaw the bow to starboard (clockwise seen from above) while the bow rises; it reverses when the bow falls.

blocks.markdown: **Gravity-driven precession of a top.** A top of mass $m$ spins fast at $\omega$ with its centre of mass a distance $h$ from the pivot. Gravity exerts a horizontal torque $mgh\sin\theta$ about the pivot, where $\theta$ is the angle of the axis from the vertical. This torque changes $\mathbf H$ not by tilting the top further, but by swinging $\mathbf H$ horizontally, so the axis precesses about the vertical at the steady rate below. The formula holds when $\omega\gg\omega_p$ (**fast-spin approximation**) and $I$ is the spin inertia. Here $\omega_p$ is the rate at which the axis circles the vertical, and $mgh\sin\theta=I\omega\,\omega_p\sin\theta$ so $\theta$ cancels.

blocks.caption: Steady precession rate of a fast-spinning top or gyroscope (rad/s), with $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$.

blocks.title: Precession of a spinning top
blocks.prompt: A top has mass 0.3 kg, $I=1.5\times10^{-4}$ kg m$^2$ about its axis and its centre of mass 0.04 m from the tip. It spins at 3000 rev/min. Find its precession rate.
blocks.answer: $\omega_p=2.50$ rad/s (about 24 rev/min); the ratio $\omega_p/\omega=0.008$ confirms the fast-spin approximation.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: A faster spin gives a slower precession, because a larger $\mathbf H$ is harder to turn. The precession axis is vertical and the top moves horizontally in the direction of the applied torque, not in the direction of the push.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Using rev/min in $C=I\omega\omega_p$, forgetting to find the direction with vectors, and using the formula $\omega_p=mgh/(I\omega)$ for a slowly spinning top where $\omega_p$ is not small.

points: $C=I\omega\omega_p$ for perpendicular spin and precession axes; the reaction on the bearings is equal and opposite to the torque on the rotor.
Direction: torque on rotor $=\boldsymbol\omega_p\times\mathbf H$, with right-hand rules for $\mathbf H$ and $\boldsymbol\omega_p$.
A top or gyroscope under gravity precesses at $\omega_p=mgh/(I\omega)$ for fast spin.

questions.stem: A rotor spins about a horizontal axis. If its axis is turned about an axis parallel to the spin axis, so that the direction of $\mathbf H$ does not change, what is the gyroscopic couple?

distractorRationale.b: This formula assumes perpendicular spin and precession axes.
distractorRationale.d: The couple is maximum when the axes are perpendicular.

questions.explanation: The torque is $\boldsymbol\omega_p\times\mathbf H$, and the cross product of parallel vectors is zero. Turning a rotor about its own spin axis only changes its spin rate, not the direction of $\mathbf H$.

questions.stem: A flywheel rotor with $I=0.35$ kg m$^2$ spins at 1800 rev/min on a frame that turns about a perpendicular axis at 0.5 rad/s. Find the gyroscopic couple in N m.

A gyroscope rotor ($I=0.04$ kg m$^2$) spins at 6000 rev/min. A reaction couple of 12 N m is measured on its mounting while its frame precesses about an axis perpendicular to the spin axis. Find the precession rate in rad/s.

A turbine rotor has its angular momentum $\mathbf H$ pointing toward the bow of a ship. The reaction couple on the ship while the bow rises is a clockwise yaw (bow to starboard) seen from above. What is the effect while the bow falls with the same spin?

options.text: The same reaction, yawing the bow to starboard
No reaction, because the bow is moving downward
A reaction that rolls the ship about its longitudinal axis
The reaction couple reverses, tending to yaw the bow to port

questions.correctOptionText: The reaction couple reverses, tending to yaw the bow to port

distractorRationale.a: Reversing the precession direction reverses the couple.
distractorRationale.b: The couple depends on the rate of turning of the axis, not on its sign.
distractorRationale.c: The couple axis is perpendicular to both the spin axis (longitudinal) and the pitching axis (transverse), i.e. vertical.

questions.explanation: Reversing $\boldsymbol\omega_p$ with $\mathbf H$ unchanged reverses $\boldsymbol\omega_p\times\mathbf H$. The couple axis remains vertical, so the yaw tendency switches from starboard to port.

questions.stem: A top has mass 0.5 kg, $I=4.0\times10^{-4}$ kg m$^2$ about its spin axis and a centre of mass 0.06 m from its pivot. It spins fast at 2400 rev/min. Find the steady precession rate in rad/s (take $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).
A spinning top precesses at a steady rate. If its spin speed is doubled with everything else unchanged, what happens to the precession rate (fast-spin approximation)?

distractorRationale.a: Precession rate is inversely proportional to the angular momentum.
distractorRationale.d: The relation is not quadratic in $\omega$.

questions.explanation: In $\omega_p=mgh/(I\omega)$ the spin speed appears in the denominator, so doubling $\omega$ halves $\omega_p$. Physically, a larger $\mathbf H$ is harder to turn with the same gravity torque.

questions.stem: A bicycle-wheel gyroscope has $I=0.25$ kg m$^2$ and spins at 600 rev/min. Its axle is horizontal, the pivot is at one end, the wheel's centre of mass is 0.30 m from the pivot and the wheel mass is 2.5 kg. Find the steady precession rate in rad/s about the vertical axis (fast-spin approximation, $g=9.81$ m/s$^2$).
questions.explanation: $\omega=600(2\pi)/60=62.83$ rad/s. The gravity torque is $mgh=2.5(9.81)(0.30)=7.36$ N m, so $\omega_p=7.36/(0.25\times62.83)=0.468$ rad/s.

questions.stem: Which statement about the direction of the gyroscopic reaction on the bearings is correct?

options.text: The reaction is unchanged by reversing the spin sense
The reaction always acts along the spin axis
Reversing either the spin sense or the precession sense reverses the reaction; reversing both leaves it unchanged
The reaction reverses only when both the spin and the precession are reversed

questions.correctOptionText: Reversing either the spin sense or the precession sense reverses the reaction; reversing both leaves it unchanged

distractorRationale.a: $\mathbf H$ flips with the spin, so the cross product flips.
distractorRationale.b: It is a couple with its axis perpendicular to the spin axis.
distractorRationale.d: Reversing both gives two sign changes, which cancel.

questions.explanation: Since $\mathbf M=\boldsymbol\omega_p\times\mathbf H$ is linear in each vector, flipping one flips the result and flipping both restores it. The couple axis is perpendicular to both.

questions.stem: Outline the vector method for finding the direction of the gyroscopic reaction couple on the bearings of a spinning rotor whose axis is being turned, and illustrate it for a rotor with $\mathbf H$ along $+x$ and a precession about $+y$.
markingGuide: Find $\mathbf H$ using the right-hand rule on the spin direction
Find $\boldsymbol\omega_p$ by the right-hand rule for the turning of the axis
Reaction on the bearings and frame is the negative of this torque
Example: $\hat j\times\hat i=-\hat k$, so torque on rotor along $-z$ and reaction on bearings along $+z$
questions.explanation: The vector method avoids guesswork about which way a gyroscope 'wants' to turn. The torque on the rotor makes $\mathbf H$ swing toward $\boldsymbol\omega_p\times\mathbf H$.

questions.stem: Derive the steady precession rate $\omega_p=mgh/(I\omega)$ for a fast-spinning top whose axis makes angle $\theta$ to the vertical, and explain why the top does not simply fall over.
markingGuide: Gravity torque about the pivot is $mgh\sin\theta$, horizontal and perpendicular to the vertical plane containing the axis
Horizontal component of $\mathbf H$ has magnitude $I\omega\sin\theta$ and rotates about the vertical at $\omega_p$
Rate of change of $\mathbf H$ is $I\omega\sin\theta\,\omega_p$
Explains that the torque changes the direction of $\mathbf H$ horizontally (precession) instead of increasing the tilt; assumptions: fast spin, steady state, $I$ about the spin axis
questions.explanation: The weight torque is perpendicular to $\mathbf H$, so it turns $\mathbf H$ rather than changing its magnitude. The top falls only when its spin decays so that $\omega_p$ becomes large and the fast-spin assumption fails.
